lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I should be ranked ahead of you, Libyan. I’m the better man.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: No. I should.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Then let Minos judge it.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: And who are you two?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: This is Hannibal the Carthaginian. I am Alexander, son of Philip.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: By Zeus. Famous men, both of you. What is the quarrel about?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Precedence. He says he was a better general than I was. I say—as everyone knows—that in war I surpassed not only him, but practically everyone before me.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Then speak in turn. You first, Libyan.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: This, for one thing, has been useful to me, Minos: down here I have learned Greek. So he cannot even have that advantage over me. I say the men most deserving of praise are those who start with nothing and still rise to greatness by their own ability, acquiring power and proving themselves fit to command.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: I set out first for Iberia with only a few men, serving as my brother’s lieutenant. I was judged the best and entrusted with the greatest responsibilities. I conquered the Celtiberians, defeated the western Gauls, crossed the great mountains, overran everything around the Eridanus, uprooted city after city, subdued the plains of Italy, and came right up to the suburbs of the leading city. In a single day I killed so many men that their rings were measured out by the bushel and rivers were bridged with corpses.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: And I did all this without being called the son of Ammon, without pretending to be a god, without retailing my mother’s dreams. I admitted I was a man. I measured myself against the shrewdest generals and fought the toughest soldiers—not Medes and Armenians who run before anyone is chasing them and hand victory to the first man bold enough to ask.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: Alexander inherited his father’s kingdom, enlarged it, and stretched it a long way, with Fortune pushing from behind. Once he had beaten that ruin of a man Darius at Issus and Arbela, he abandoned Macedonian habits, demanded to be worshipped, converted himself to Median luxury, murdered his friends at dinner, and arrested them for execution.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: I governed my own country on equal terms. And when I was recalled because the enemy had sailed against Libya with a great fleet, I obeyed at once. I made myself a private citizen; when I was condemned, I accepted it sensibly. And I did all this as a barbarian, without Greek education, not reciting Homer like him, not trained by Aristotle the sophist, but using only my own good nature.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: That is why I say I am better than Alexander. If this man is handsomer because he tied a ribbon round his head, perhaps Macedonians find that impressive. But it would not make him seem superior to a brave and general-like man who relied more on judgment than on luck.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: He has made a respectable speech for himself—better than one might have expected from a Libyan. Alexander, what do you say to that?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Strictly speaking, Minos, I ought not to answer a man this insolent. My reputation is enough to teach you what sort of king I was, and what sort of bandit he was. Still, consider whether I surpassed him point by point.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I was still young when I came to power, took control of a kingdom in turmoil, and punished my father’s murderers. Then, after frightening Greece with the destruction of Thebes, I was elected general by the Greeks themselves. I did not think it enough to sit in Macedonia and lovingly preserve the rule my father left me. I conceived the whole earth as my object, and thought it shameful if I failed to master all of it.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: So I invaded Asia with a small force. I won a great battle at the Granicus; I took Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia, and everything else as it came under my feet, until I reached Issus, where Darius stood his ground with many tens of thousands of troops.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: What happened after that, Minos, you people know: how many dead I sent down to you in a single day. The ferryman says his boat was not enough for them; most had to lash rafts together and make their own crossing.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And I did all this while taking the first risk myself and being willing to be wounded. Not to bore you with Tyre or Arbela: I went as far as India, made Ocean the boundary of my empire, captured their elephants, and subdued Porus. I crossed the Tanais and defeated the Scythians—no negligible men—in a great cavalry battle. I rewarded my friends and punished my enemies.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And if people thought I was a god, they may be forgiven for believing something of the kind about me, given the scale of my achievements.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Finally: I died as a king. This man died in exile at the court of Prusias the Bithynian, which was just what he deserved, being the most unscrupulous and savage of men. As for how he defeated the Italians—I will pass over the fact that it was not by strength, but by villainy, bad faith, and tricks, with nothing lawful or open about it.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And since he reproached me with luxury, he seems to have forgotten what he did at Capua, keeping company with courtesans and, admirable man, squandering the opportunities of war in pleasure.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: If I had not thought the western lands too small and turned my ambition eastward instead, what great thing would it have been for me to take Italy without bloodshed, add Libya, and bring everything as far as Gades under my power? Those places already crouched low and acknowledged a master; they did not seem worth fighting.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I have spoken. Judge, Minos. This is enough from many possible proofs.

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: Not before you hear me too.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: And who are you, my excellent man? Where are you from, that you will speak?

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: Scipio, an Italian general: the man who brought down Carthage and defeated the Libyans in great battles.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: And what will you say?

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: That I am inferior to Alexander, but superior to Hannibal. I defeated him, drove him out, and forced him to flee in disgrace. So how is this man not shameless, competing with Alexander, when I—Scipio, the man who beat him—do not think myself fit to be compared with Alexander?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: By Zeus, Scipio, that is a fair-minded statement. So let Alexander be judged first; after him, you; and then, if we like, Hannibal third—though he too is not to be despised.
